newsitem.title: USA: Senate easily approves balanced budget measure.
newsitem.headline: Senate easily approves balanced budget measure.

text.p: Capping months of tough negotiations and heated rhetoric, the Senate on Thursday overwhelmingly approved legislation to balance the budget by 2002, sending it to President Bill Clinton for his signature.
A united Senate passed the bill by a bipartisan 85-15 vote then quickly turned to a companion measure cutting taxes by a net $95 billion over five years.
The House passed the tax measure 389-43 on Thursday providing a $500-per-child credit, cutting the capital gains rate and providing breaks for higher education.
Republican leaders want to deliver both bills to the White House before adjourning on Friday for a month-long recess.

"On both sides of the aisle and both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue, Republicans and Democrats, House and Senate and, yes, the president are all saying, 'This is good for America,'" said Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi.
Lott told senators he was humming "Hail to the Chief" in honour of the deal.
The budget legislation reduces Medicare and Medicaid spending, creates a new children's health programme and restores some spending cuts in a landmark welfare law.
Clinton hailed approval as "the achievement of a generation and a triumph for every American."
"This budget marks an end to decades of deficits and just as important, it honours our values," he said in a statement.
Victory was sweet for both sides.

Republicans have long made balancing the budget a top priority. That goal appeared out of reach in 1995 when party leaders forced an unpopular government shutdown in a failed effort to get Clinton to agree to a more sweeping budget plan.

Without a single Republican vote Clinton in 1993 pushed budget legislation through Congress raising taxes and cutting spending. Democrats believe that tough vote was a major reason they lost control of Congress.
Helped along by a robust economy that sliced the deficit, and let them to sidestep some tough spending decisions, the two sides finally came together on this year's budget deal.
While the Senate vote was lopsided, there was some grumbling. Twelve of the Senate's 55 Republicans voted no, along with three of its 45 Democrats.

Some conservatives opponents, including Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm, complained the legislation did not go nearly far enough to rein in long-term entitlements, while creating an expensive new children's health plan.
"It (children's health) has already grown to $24 billion before we adopt the bill. Does anybody believe this programme is not going to explode in the future?" Gramm said.
Democratic Sen. Paul Wellstone of Minnesota has said the measure goes too far, cutting Medicare and other social programmes to fund tax cuts that would mainly aid the well-off.
Some senators voted against the bill because it included a 15-cents-per-pack increase in the federal cigarette tax.

Despite the rhetoric, the legislation by itself would not bring the budget into balance. The measure cuts spending on mandatory programmes such as Medicare and Medicaid by about $130 billion over five years.
It directs Congress to find another $140 billion in reductions over that same period as part of annual spending bills, but does not specify where they are to come from.
Critics charged future Congresses will never muster the political will to cut veterans, education, nutrition and other social programmes, making the bill an empty promise.
The legislation reduces Medicare by about $115 billion over five years, largely by cutting payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers.

Beneficiaries would see monthly premiums rise to $67 in 2002 from $43.80 this year. They would have an expanded menu of preventive benefits and more insurance choices -- including tax-free medical savings accounts opposed by the White House.

Lawmakers included $24 billion in grants to states to expand health care to the 10 million uninsured U.S. children. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the plan will cover about 2 million previously uninsured children.
The White House won welfare spending, restoring aid to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants, creating a $3 billion welfare-to-work programme and easing Food Stamp cuts.
Medicaid insurance for the poor, elderly and disabled would fall by more than $13 billion. Most of the savings come from trimming aid to hospitals serving indigent patients.
The measure includes calls on regulators to auction off part of the public broadcast spectrum, raising $21 billion."
